title: Our repos and how a ticket is written

story: Your first platform ticket arrives: "[Platform] Broker: per-run capabilities and one-repo GitHub tokens". You know the product repo well, so you open fcp and search for broker. You find a workflow that calls Byte, our review agent, from another repo, and nothing else. Twenty minutes later you still do not know where the new code goes, how it will be deployed, or who has to approve it.

The broker is a fair example of why this is confusing. Its new code, the code it starts from, and its deployment live in three different repos, and the branches it pushes land in a fourth. Every ticket in the plan points at files somewhere, and the plan touches nine repos.
hook.question: Given any ticket, how do I tell which repo it lands in, and how do I read the ticket so I can start without asking anyone?

p: Three repos hold almost everything, and one question each tells them apart. Is it the product that customers run? Then it is fcp, the monorepo you know, with the backend in cloud/, the on-prem client in client/, the Python SDK in sdk/, the dashboard in frontend/ and shared code in common/. Nova, our agent that turns Jira tickets into pull requests, opens its PRs here, but the platform itself never lives here.

Is it the platform's own code? Then it is ai-agents, a new TypeScript repo with one npm workspace per service: the gateway, the broker, the orchestrator, the harness that runs inside each machine, the Slack app and the required checks, plus folders that hold only data, such as the routines' charters.

Is it a machine, a network, a secret's path or the deployment of a service? Then it is infrastructure, written in OpenTofu (the open-source version of Terraform) and Terragrunt (a tool that keeps many small OpenTofu folders consistent). It also holds the image every agent machine starts from and the units that run our services on inf, our internal Kubernetes cluster.

The other repos are smaller and easy to place. gitops holds Helm charts (packages of Kubernetes files) and the settings for Argo CD, a tool inside each product cluster that installs whatever the repo describes. It serves the product clusters only, so nothing of the agent platform is deployed from it. byte is Byte's code, and its broker is where ours starts. claude-plugins is a new private marketplace of skills and hooks that people and agents load. The R&D brain, the reviewed pages about our systems, is split in two: rnd-kb holds the pages, and rnd-kb-tooling holds the Python tools that check, search and answer from them. Last, fcp-local-lab holds FCP Lab, the whole product running on one machine with fake data, where people and agents test a change before it reaches a real environment.

code.text:
repo             what lives there                                  language
fcp              the product: cloud/ client/ sdk/ frontend/ common/  Python, TypeScript
ai-agents        the platform: gateway/ broker/ orchestrator/       TypeScript
                 harness/ slack-app/ checks/, data folders, evals/  (evals/ is Python)
infrastructure   accounts, network, proxy, machine image, warm      OpenTofu, Terragrunt,
                 pools, and the deployments of our services on inf  Packer
gitops           Argo CD apps and Helm charts for product clusters  YAML
byte             Byte, our review agent                             TypeScript
claude-plugins   skills and hooks that people and agents load       Markdown, small hooks
rnd-kb           the brain's pages and its data rules               Markdown
rnd-kb-tooling   the brain's tools: page linter, search, Slack bot  Python
fcp-local-lab    FCP Lab: the whole product on one machine          shell, Markdown

notes.text: No CODEOWNERS file, so any engineer may review any folder; the rules on main ask for exactly one approval. Releases are published by CI, which updates gitops.
New this quarter: the plan creates it in week 2. Its CI builds one image per service, and infrastructure then deploys those images.
Owned by DevOps: every change needs a DevOps approval, and a person runs plan and apply. Agents never apply.
Only for the product clusters. No Argo CD app deploys to inf, so our services are never deployed from here.
New this quarter: the plan creates it in week 3. It is private; the public repo of skills is for customers.

p: Back to the broker. Its new code is TypeScript in ai-agents, in the broker workspace. It does not start from zero: Byte already has a broker that holds a GitHub token and gives the review worker only a short-lived pass, and that code has passed a security review and has tests. So the ticket copies Byte's broker into ai-agents and extends it, while Byte keeps its own copy for now. Byte's repo is read, not changed.

The broker runs on inf, and everything that runs on inf is deployed from infrastructure, as a helm_release unit (a small file in Terraform's language, run by OpenTofu, that installs a Helm chart on the cluster). That deployment is a separate ticket for DevOps, a few weeks later, because it can only use an image that already exists. The broker's most sensitive input, the private key of the agents' GitHub App, is not in any repo at all: it sits in Vault, our secret store, and only the broker reads it.

code.text:
ai-agents/broker/src/scopes.ts                 the new code: run scopes, one-repo tokens
byte/src/broker.ts                             the starting point, copied and extended
infrastructure/multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/ai-agents/broker/
                                               the deployment on inf: a helm_release unit
Vault: infrastructure/ai-agents/github-app     the GitHub App's key, read only by the broker
fcp, branch nova/RH-1234                       where the broker's pushes land

notes.text: The platform team writes this in week 3. This is the ticket from the story.
Read and copied, not changed. A security-reviewed starting point saves days.
DevOps, weeks 5 and 6, in the infrastructure repo: one more pull request, with its own reviewers.
Vault is a secret store, not a repo. The key is stored there in week 2 and never reaches a machine that runs an agent.
The broker pushes Nova's branch for every run, but no platform code lives in fcp.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why one run never changes two repos
p: The broker gives each run a GitHub token for exactly one repo, so a single agent run can never change ai-agents and fcp together, or infrastructure and anything else. A change that needs two repos becomes two tickets and two pull requests, each with its own CI and its own reviewer. That is slower for a person, and it is on purpose for an agent: one repo per run keeps a fooled run from reaching further than the one place it was given.

read.h: The path usually names the repo
p: Every ticket that produces code shows the path of its key file, and that path is your fastest clue. Paths are written in three ways. Some start with the repo's name, such as ai-agents/broker/src/scopes.ts. Some start inside a repo, such as cloud/rhinoCloud/tests_api/conftest.py or modules/aws-sandbox-pool/asg.tf. And some add a note in brackets, such as src/review.ts (RhinoHealth/byte).

So it pays to know each repo's top folders. cloud/, client/, sdk/, frontend/ and common/ mean fcp. modules/, terraform/, multi_tenant/ and packer/ mean infrastructure. A note in brackets always wins over the folder, because src/ and scripts/ exist in several repos. When neither helps, as with a path that starts with .github/workflows/, a folder that every repo has, the ticket's How steps name the repo. In the lab you turn these rules into a small function and run it over all 242 tickets.

read.h: Reading a ticket: What, Why, How and a sketch
p: Every ticket has the same shape, so once you can read one, you can read all of them. The title starts with the owning team in brackets and says what the ticket delivers, in about 75 characters at most. What says in one or two sentences what gets built or decided. Why says what goes wrong, or stays slow, without it; it is the sentence you repeat when someone asks why you are doing this. How is a list of practical steps with real paths, commands and names. Most tickets end with a code sketch: the key file, 6 to 35 lines, written with real library calls.

There are no acceptance criteria and no "done when" list. You know you are done when the What exists and the problem in the Why no longer happens, and the How is the route there. Two more rules save you time. A sketch shows the shape of the file, not finished code: when it disagrees with the library's documentation, the documentation wins, and you mention the difference in your pull request. And a step or a comment that says decide, or confirm with a named person, is an open question with an owner, so you ask before you build.

notes.text: [Team], then what it delivers. From the title alone you know who owns it and what exists afterwards.
What: the deliverable, and here also the repo (ai-agents/broker) and the starting point (Byte's broker).
Why: the problem it removes. Agents never hold keys, so something outside the machine must.
How: steps with real paths. This one tells you to start from Byte's code and its tests.
The sketch: the path of the key file is your best clue to the repo.

deeper.h: Go deeper: names that confuse people
p: In the product, agent already means something else: the Rhino Client, the on-premises part of the product that runs at customer sites, appears as rhinoAgent in the code and as machines such as rhino-agent-qa-1. To avoid confusion, everything about AI agents is called ai-agents: the repo, the AWS account, the Temporal namespace, the GitHub App rhino-ai-agents and the machine image ai-agent-sandbox.

Inside ai-agents, file names use kebab-case, such as ticket-to-pr.ts and git-proxy.ts, while the Python in evals/ keeps snake_case. Names that other code depends on, such as environment variables, HTTP paths, JSON fields and YAML keys, never change once a ticket defines them.

lab.title: Which repo does this ticket land in?
lab.goal: Recognise each repo by its folders, and write a function that tells you which repo any ticket's code lands in.

guess.q: Every ticket with code shows the path of its key file. If you group the 242 tickets by the first folder of that path, is each group one repo?

options.text: Yes: the first folder is always the name of the repo.
options.why: Many paths start inside a repo, such as cloud/ or modules/, so the first folder is often a folder, not a repo.

options.text: No: many paths start inside a repo, so you must know each repo's top folders and read the notes in brackets.
options.why: cloud/ means fcp and modules/ means infrastructure, and src/ needs the note in brackets because several repos have one.

options.text: No: the paths are random and say nothing useful about the repo.
options.why: The paths are real. With a few rules they place about nine tickets out of ten.

lab.build: Write where.mjs with a function repoOf(file) that turns a sketch path into a repo name, and use it to count the tickets per repo. The rules, in this order: no path means "no code: a decision"; a note in brackets that names a repo wins, with or without RhinoHealth/ in front, such as (RhinoHealth/byte) or (gitops repo); a first folder that is a repo name is that repo; cloud, client, sdk, frontend, common, scripts and pyproject.toml mean fcp; modules, terraform, multi_tenant and packer mean infrastructure; anything else is "unknown: read the How". Print one line per repo with its count, biggest first.
checks: node where.mjs prints 99 for ai-agents, 29 for infrastructure and 24 for fcp.
byte gets 16 tickets: 15 found through the notes in brackets, and one whose path starts with byte/.
16 tickets show as no code: a decision.
22 tickets stay unknown, and for two of them, picked at random, you can name the repo by reading their How steps.
repoOf("scripts/gold-mine.ts (RhinoHealth/byte)") gives byte, and repoOf("modules/aws-sandbox-pool/asg.tf") gives infrastructure.
lab.fix: A teammate wrote the same rules but checked the folders before the note in brackets. Their count says fcp 26 and byte 14, and a planning sheet built from it puts two of Byte's scripts in the product repo, where nobody will ever find them. Find which two paths moved and explain why the note in brackets has to be read first.
explain: The broker's new code, its starting point and its deployment live in three repos. Name them, and say which team changes each one and why the deployment comes later.
Why does the first folder of a path sometimes fail to name the repo, and what do you read then?
Our tickets have no acceptance criteria. How do you decide that a ticket is done?
lab.done: where.mjs puts 99 tickets in ai-agents, 29 in infrastructure and 24 in fcp, and for any new ticket you can say which repo it lands in and who has to approve it.

check.q: Where does the Helm release that runs the broker on inf live?

options.text: In gitops, as an Argo CD app next to the product's services.
options.why: gitops deploys the product clusters only. No Argo CD app deploys to inf.

options.text: In infrastructure, as a Terraform helm_release unit, owned by DevOps.
options.why: Everything that runs on inf is deployed from the infrastructure repo, and a person runs the apply.

options.text: In ai-agents, next to the broker's code.
options.why: ai-agents builds the code and its image. The deployment that runs the image lives in infrastructure.

check.q: A ticket's sketch path is modules/aws-egress-proxy/templates/squid.conf.tpl. Which repo is it, and who has to approve the pull request?

options.text: infrastructure, and a DevOps engineer must approve it.
options.why: modules/ is a top folder of infrastructure, and that repo's CODEOWNERS file asks for DevOps on every change.

options.text: ai-agents, and any engineer may approve it.
options.why: ai-agents paths start with the workspace name, such as broker/ or harness/. modules/ belongs to infrastructure.

options.text: fcp, because the proxy protects the product.
options.why: The proxy protects the agent machines, and machines and networks are described in infrastructure.

check.q: A How step says "Decide with Security how the sandbox machines reach this service." What do you do?

options.text: Pick the option that is quickest to build and explain it in the pull request.
options.why: The choice affects walls that other goals rely on. It is not yours to make alone.

options.text: Add acceptance criteria to the ticket so the reviewer knows what to check.
options.why: Our tickets have no acceptance criteria. An open question is settled by its owner, not by more text.

options.text: Ask the named owner, write the decision into the ticket, then build.
options.why: decide marks an open question with an owner. Asking first costs an hour; guessing can cost a rewrite.

p: Every platform ticket in this course names its key file, and the walkthrough lessons follow those files repo by repo. The tickets below create the repos this lesson describes, and the broker ticket is the running example of one feature spread over three repos.
The rule that a run's token covers exactly one repo is enforced by the broker, and you build it in the runtime walkthrough.

tickets.why: Creates the ai-agents repo: npm workspaces, CI and the rules on main.
The broker: the running example, code in ai-agents, starting from Byte's broker.
Deploys the broker and the other services on inf from the infrastructure repo.
Creates claude-plugins, the private marketplace of skills and hooks.
Lays out rnd-kb, the repo of the brain's pages.

words.plain: The product monorepo: cloud/, client/, sdk/, frontend/ and common/. Agents' pull requests land here.
The new TypeScript repo of the platform: gateway, broker, orchestrator, harness, Slack app and checks.
OpenTofu and Terragrunt for our cloud, the machine image, and the deployments of services on inf. DevOps approves.
A small Terraform file in infrastructure that installs a Helm chart on the inf cluster.
Our ticket format: what gets built, why it matters, practical steps, plus a code sketch. No acceptance criteria.
The shape of a ticket's key file with real APIs. Its path is the best clue to the repo.

review.q: From memory, name the repo for each: a Temporal workflow, a VPC, a brain page, a skill, a Django test, Byte's review prompt.
review.a: ai-agents (orchestrator), infrastructure, rnd-kb, claude-plugins, fcp (cloud/), byte.

review.q: Write the order of rules in repoOf and say why the note in brackets comes before the folders.
review.a: No path, then the note in brackets, then a repo-named first folder, then fcp folders, then infrastructure folders, else unknown. src/ and scripts/ exist in several repos, so only the note can tell them apart.

review.q: A teammate asks where to change the broker's memory limit. What do you answer?
review.a: In its deployment, the helm_release unit in infrastructure under multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/ai-agents/broker/, approved by DevOps; not in ai-agents, which only builds the code and image.

remember: Agents work in fcp, the platform lives in ai-agents, machines and deployments live in infrastructure, and a ticket reads as What, Why, How and a sketch whose path names the repo.
